title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what the guide really claims

questions.prompt: Your book prints a model sentence about Scotland: "Scotland is one of the constituent countries of the United Kingdom. It occupies the northern third of the island of Great Britain and shares a land border to the south with England." Write the same two sentences about WALES. Which imitation keeps the structure of the model AND the map right?

options.text: Wales is one of the constituent countries of Great Britain. It occupies the western side of the United Kingdom and shares a land border to the east with England.
Wales is one of the constituent countries of the United Kingdom. It occupies the eastern side of the island of Great Britain and shares a land border to the west with England.
Wales is one of the constituent countries of the United Kingdom. It occupies the western side of the island of Great Britain and shares a land border to the east with England.
Wales is one of the constituent countries of the United Kingdom. It occupies the southern third of the island of Ireland and shares a land border to the north with England.

questions.explanation: Imitating a model means keeping its three moves and changing only what the map changes. Move one names the whole: Wales is one of the constituent countries of the United Kingdom — of the state, not of the island, because Great Britain has no constituent countries, it simply carries three of them. Move two places the country inside the island: Wales lies along the western side of Great Britain, with the sea on that side and England on the other. Move three names the neighbour and the side it is on, and since England is to the east of Wales, the land border is to the east. Putting Wales in the eastern half turns the map round, and putting it on the island of Ireland moves it across a sea.

questions.prompt: A poster outside a palace reads: "the changing of the guard — one of the world's most spectacular ceremonies". A journalist wants to show that the poster is exaggerating. Which finding would actually damage the claim?

options.text: A ceremony held every March in Bangkok is far more spectacular than this one.
The ceremony lasts forty-five minutes, much longer than most visitors expect it to.
On some winter mornings the ceremony is cancelled because of heavy snowfall.
Writers who rank the world's ceremonies put this one outside their top twenty.

questions.explanation: One of the most spectacular claims membership of a top group, not the top place — so the only way to damage it is to show that the ceremony does not belong to that group at all, which is exactly what a ranking that leaves it far down the list does. Finding a more spectacular ceremony in Bangkok damages nothing: the poster never said there was none above it, and that is why writers of advertisements love the phrase. It sounds enormous and it is almost impossible to disprove. The length of the ceremony and the mornings when snow cancels it say nothing at all about how spectacular it is when it does take place.

questions.prompt: A trainee guide has written four sentences about the castle. His teacher asks for a paragraph that DESCRIBES and does nothing else — no persuading anywhere in it. Which sentence must go?

options.text: Do not leave this town without climbing up here: you will remember it for ever.
The castle stands on a rock above the town and was begun in the twelfth century.
From the terrace you can see the whole of the old town and the sea beyond it.
The rooms on the north side are the coldest in the building, even in July.

questions.explanation: Persuading is recognised by its direction: the sentence turns round and faces the reader. An imperative tells him what to do, and a promise tells him what he will get — that is a piece of selling, and it has no place in a paragraph that only describes. The three others keep their eyes on the castle. Two of them give facts anybody can check, and the third is the one that catches people out: the coldest rooms in the building is a superlative, and a superlative is not persuasion by itself. It compares rooms with rooms, it can be checked with a thermometer, and it invites nobody anywhere.

questions.prompt: A guide sums up tomorrow's walk out loud, but not in the order the group will walk it: "The coach park is where the walk ends. We meet under the stone arch on the main square. Once the cathedral is behind us we go down to the botanical garden. The covered market comes before the cathedral, not after it." Put the five stops in the order the group will reach them.

options.text: the cathedral
the coach park
the stone arch on the main square
the botanical garden
the covered market

questions.explanation: Nothing here is numbered and no time is given: the order is carried entirely by four small relational words, and they have to be collected out of the order in which they were said. We meet under the stone arch fixes the start. Comes before the cathedral, not after it puts the covered market second and the cathedral third. Once the cathedral is behind us hangs the botanical garden onto the cathedral, so it comes fourth. And is where the walk ends sends the coach park to the very end, however early it was mentioned. That is how a guide really speaks, and it is how a route has to be rebuilt: listen for before, after, once and ends, not for the order of the sentences.

questions.prompt: A brochure ends on this line: "Every August the festival revives the old town." From that one verb a careful reader learns something about the town in the other eleven months. What?

options.text: The old town stays closed to visitors outside the month of August.
For most of the year the old town is quiet and half empty.
The festival has been held in the old town for a very long time.
The old town was destroyed at some point and has been rebuilt.

questions.explanation: To revive is to bring back to life something that had gone still, so the verb carries its own hidden half: you only revive what was quiet. The brochure never says the town is empty for eleven months — it lets the reader work it out, which is why a careful reader must. Closed to visitors goes much further than the word allows, since a quiet town is still open. Nothing in the verb dates the festival, and nothing in it says a stone was ever knocked down: reviving a town is about its life, not about its walls. Verbs of this kind are worth hunting for in a text, because what they take for granted is often what the writer would rather not print.

questions.prompt:
Here is a whole ad, and nothing else is known about the walk:

CITY WALKS — THE OLD HARBOUR ROUTE
Every day at 9.00 am · Departs from the clock tower, North Gate
Ends at the ferry terminal · About two hours on foot
On the way: the fish auction, the lighthouse, the Sailors' Chapel
FREE — no ticket, no booking

Tick EVERY statement that the ad actually PROVES. Leave the others, however likely they sound.

options.text: Somebody who turns up on a Sunday morning will find the walk running.
The visitor pays nothing at all to take part in the walk.
The group finishes the walk at the point where it started.
The fish auction is going on while the group walks past it.
The group is normally back on the street before midday.

questions.explanation: Every day covers Sunday, so the first statement is printed in all but name. Free, with no ticket and no booking, settles the price at nothing. And nine o'clock plus about two hours puts the group back on the street around eleven, comfortably before midday — the arithmetic is in the ad, so the ad proves it. The other two are what the reader supplies himself. The walk departs from the clock tower and ends at the ferry terminal, two different places, so it does not come back to its starting point. And on the way: the fish auction proves only that the route passes the auction; whether anything is being sold at nine in the morning is a question the ad never touches. An ad proves what it prints, never what it lets you imagine.
